definition: A populist is a political figure who claims to champion ordinary people against a privileged elite.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word populist. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know populist should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The mayor's populist streak showed in every speech — potholes and grocery prices, never a word for the bond markets.
A maverick is a milder figure than a populist: mavericks merely go their own way inside the system, while a populist builds the whole platform on the people's fight against an elite.
Demagogue goes further than populist — a populist claims the people's cause; a demagogue inflames the crowd's worst fears, usually with falsehoods, to take power for himself.

A demagogue whips up the crowd's fears and prejudices, usually with lies, to seize power. A populist claims the people's side against an elite — a stance, not a verdict: a populist's case can be honest.
A reformer wants the system fixed and may work from any position — expert panels included. A populist adds the frame: the people against the elite, with the speaker on the people's side.

In the 1890s, ruined wheat farmers built a party around a single message — the railroads and the eastern banks were fleecing the plains — and the press called them populists.
The label fit: the whole platform was the many against the moneyed few.
A populist stakes out one particular fight: ordinary people against a privileged elite.
The word marks that stance, not the speaker's honesty — a populist may be a sincere reformer or a cynical vote-hunter.
What it never means is simply 'well liked': plenty of populists lose elections, and plenty of beloved politicians never touch the people-versus-elite theme.

Populist and populace are the pair to keep straight: the populace is the people themselves; a populist is a politician who claims to fight for them.
Use populist for the stance — people versus elite — and reach for demagogue only when the method is fear and falsehood.
And resist the schoolroom slip: populist never means simply 'popular.'

Historians still argue about Governor Ada Reyes, who swept into office in 1934 on a wave of small-town anger.
Her critics called her reckless; her admirers called her the only honest voice in the capital.
Both camps agreed she was a populist.
Every speech set the same scene: farm families and mill hands on one side, the railroad barons and their hired legislators on the other.
Unlike some who used that script, she never invented villains or figures — auditors later confirmed the freight overcharges she attacked were real.
Whether her rate caps helped or hurt is still debated, but no one disputes whose side she claimed: the people's, against the few who ran the state.
